utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom, and to those who are listening to us. Before the next witness is being brought in, I would like to raise three procedural matters. The first one is related to the sitting schedule of this week. The president of this Tribunal has scheduled a plenary of all judges on Wednesday this week. That means the day after tomorrow, in the morning, between 9.00 and at least 12.00. We will not be able to sit on Wednesday because there is no courtroom available in the afternoon. So that the hearing on Wednesday must be cancelled. We will liaise with the parties today or tomorrow how to proceed. I think we have to take into consideration if we would be able to sit, instead of Wednesday, Friday in the afternoon, but we have to figure out the possibilities for that. We will come back to that problem later. I turn now to the second problem. The Chamber has been informed that the public versions of the transcripts for 92 quater witnesses, Bojinovic, Deronjic, and PW-067, have been assigned 65 ter numbers, 2322A, 2326A, and 2315A, and are now admitted as Exhibits P8A, P20A, and P1A respectively. Last Friday, I asked the Defence to provide us with a specific request during our today's hearing what we should consider as additional time and what amount of time for the preparation of the cross-examination of Mr. Blaszczyk is required. I would like now to ask the Defence what is the specific request. Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I greet everybody present in the courtroom. May God's peace reign in this house, and may these proceedings end in keeping with God's will, and not necessarily mine. Mr. President, we don't need additional time to examine Mr. Blaszczyk, we need additional time to study 3.000 written documents. We need additional time to study the materials in order to see whether the materials are credible. They have been obtained subsequently, after the events, after the trial has already started. When you first asked about that, we told you that we needed a month and a half of working days. Some people have been granted three months, some have been granted a month. We believe that we need a month and a half since the Prosecutor said that the materials are very important due to certain information contained therein. We would like to study all of that. Thank you. Well, the documents are right there in front of us, and you can see how voluminous the documents are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your position? When will you be able to commence your cross-examination? Could you give us a date?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't understand why we don't understand each other. I can cross-examine witness Blaszczyk tomorrow, but I will not have all the information about evidence tendered through him. I don't know what was written during the war. I will not know what may have been falsified. I won't know anything. I can't study the documents in the course of the trial. I have to be given time outside of the courtroom time, which means I need a month and a half when we are not sitting in order to study the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is exactly what we wanted to know. This is the first time that I hear that you want to have an adjournment of the trial for one and a half months. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I need the Chamber not to be sitting in order to study the materials. If I could do it while the trial was ongoing I would not be asking for any additional time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, are you in the position to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon. With the lengthy holiday recess, that should, I would hope, work for at least three weeks of what the general is requesting. So I would hope we could bring Mr. Blaszczyk back near the end of January sometime, and that should be very close to what the general is asking, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber will consider the request of Mr. Tolimir and your response at a later stage and come back to the request later. If there are no other matters to raise, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome to the trial. Would you please read aloud the solemn declaration on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, for the Prosecution, will examine you now. Sorry, Mr. Elderkin. It's too early in the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honours. Good afternoon to you and to everyone else, and if I can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Witness, as you know, my name is Rupert Elderkin, and I'll be asking you a few questions this afternoon on behalf of the Prosecution. I'll start, please, by asking you to say your name.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: My name is Fredy Peccerelli.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And before we start with further questions, I see you brought a binder of some documents with you into the courtroom. Could you just tell us, so everyone in here knows, what it is that you've brought in with you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I have the report for the Lazete 1 exhumation and excavation and the Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Very good. And since we are both speaking the same language, I'd also remind you if we could both try to leave a pause between our question and answer to allow for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying here in the Popovic case in March of 2007?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And have you had a chance recently to read your Popovic trial testimony?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And does the transcript of your testimony fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today and asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, it does; I believe it reflects my answers in the same way I would answer them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I'd ask for the admission of the witness's prior testimony as well as with the previously admitted exhibits, and those I think have been premarked with P numbers, but for the record the 65 ter number of the prior testimony is 6482, and two exhibits were admitted through this witness in Popovic; 1732, which is an expert report, and 1733, which is the witness's curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These documents will be received. The Popovic transcript as P934, and the other two documents as P935 and P936. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: With Your Honour's permission, I would like to read a very short summary of the witness's prior evidence. 1

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli is a forensic anthropologist. He worked for the ICTY on the excavation and exhumation of mass graves from 1997 through to 2000. In 2000 he held the position of deputy senior director of the archaeology team, under Professor Richard Wright. He was responsible for finding a grave, recovering its contents, ensuring the chain of custody, and placing human remains recovered from the grave in a refrigerated container to be sent to the morgue in Visoko. In 2000, Mr. Peccerelli headed the team working on the Lazete 1 mass grave. The grave contained 127 bodies, and two further bodies were found in an adjacent ditch. 89 of the bodies had probable blindfolds. It was clear the bodies had previously been removed from the grave, since in some places the team only found body parts and the soil was different from in the rest of the grave. The same year, Mr. Peccerelli also supervised the excavation of part of the Lazete 2 grave, which was nearby. The grave had previously been excavated in 1996 by a team from Physicians for Human Rights, or PHR, led by Dr. Bill Haglund. In addition to the 1996 PHR excavation, it was clear that bodies had previously been removed from the grave in a robbing event since, in some places, the team only found body parts and there were truncated bodies at the edge of the robbing areas. Mr. Peccerelli's team recovered 16 bodies from the grave, as well as body parts and a large number of artefacts, mostly comprising shell casings. Your Honours, I now have some further questions for the witness, including a report on Lazete 2, which was referenced in his prior testimony but not admitted so I'd like to cover that in a little more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, could you briefly tell us a bit more about your career, starting from when you began working as a forensic archaeologist and anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I began to work in 1995 in Guatemala for the Guatemalan Forensic Anthropology Foundation. Basically, my duties were to locate, excavate and exhume bodies from mass graves in Guatemala as well as analyse the remains and try to identify them, as well as their cause of death, to subsequently then render expert reports to the Guatemalan Prosecution or Attorney General's office and eventually give back to the families the identified bodies that were recovered. Since then, I have become the executive director of the foundation. We have a 96-person team that works and has four scientific departments which are forensic archaeology, forensic anthropology, the department of the investigation of missing persons, and also forensic genetics. The foundation recently has now gone through the accreditation, ISO accreditation 17025 2005 for its forensic genetic laboratory, and during that time, I also participated in three different occasions with ICTY; in 1997 and 1998, and also in 2000, as you referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the Court has heard a little bit about DNA identification and its use in your line of work. Can you explain in basic detail whether you continue with other methods of analysis and identification or has this other work been replaced by DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Oh, no, the advances in DNA have been substantial in the last couple of years, especially since the work carried out during the bombing of the World Trade Centre in New York and also during the identification process of the victims in the Balkans. Since then, many advancements have been made, but in no way has this replaced traditional archaeology or anthropology. As a matter of fact, it has become evident in the field that DNA by itself does not produce identifications. A multi-disciplinary approach is necessary, whereby we understand the universe of the victims, understand how these victims were deposited in their graves, try to identify them and establish their individual biological profiles through anthropological analysis, and then compare all of that information with DNA findings. Now it's important to understand that DNA would only be able to identify a victim if we have either the victim's own DNA in a database or their family's DNA. So it serves just as much as ante-mortem information. In other words, to get an identification, whether it be through traditional means or DNA, you need to have something to compare the information to. In this case, it would be familial DNA. In other words, we need the investigation team to find the family members of the victims. And in order to do that, we need to understand who the victims are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to your work in Bosnia and about the two Lazete sites that you worked on. For reference, is it right that the Lazete sites are at a location close to the village of Orahovac in your understanding?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The Lazete sites are basically where the fields are located but down the road from the Orahovac school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the location of the village of Orahovac at the time you did the work on these graves?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I was -- at the time of the excavation, I was not -- I did not have the information about Orahovac per se. I later found this out after testifying here last time, that supposedly that's where -- or that's where some of the victims of Srebrenica were taken prior to them being transferred over to the Lazete sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has, in fact, had the opportunity to visit the Lazete/Orahovac location and has seen the grave sites, one close by the road junction and then another one where you pass underneath the railway line in a clearing by some trees. Could you tell us, in those reference points, which is Lazete 1 and which is Lazete 2?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Lazete 1 is the one that's by the road. It's right by the road junction, and Lazete 2 would be on the other side of the railroad tracks. Lazete 1 is the smaller site and it's a smaller grave. Lazete 2 is a much larger grave and also the grave that was exhumed previously, in 1996, by the PHR team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: For Lazete 1, when did you start work on that site?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Let's see. July 13th, 2000, to August 8th, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you please describe briefly the process of the excavation and exhumation at that site.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, during this recovery, we were very fortunate to have satellite images or aerial images that would show the field prior to some disturbance in the soil. In other words, we had an image of July 5th, 1995, and then another image later in July -- let's see if I can find it. It would be on page 11 of the Lazete 1 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Actually, if I may interrupt, if we could perhaps have the report up on the screen, it may help orientate everyone. It's 65 ter 1732, which is P935. If we can go to page 11, please. I think that's the page referenced by the witness.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Next page. That's page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: One further page, please. I think the B/C/S will be page 18. I guess that's going to be page -- the e-court page is 18. Apologies for the interruption, Mr. Peccerelli, but if you could please continue.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Sure. So as you can see in the two top images, there is a picture of July 5, 1995, with no disturbance on the field. And then there is an image right next to it, image figure 13b, showing the date of 27 July 1995 and you can see there are two disturbances, the one at the top being Lazete 1 and the one in the bottom, and larger, being Lazete 2. In the figure 14a you can see a close-up of the disturbance, so we had a very -- we had a hypothesis of where this grave was located in the field. We later decided to scrape off the top layer of soils. We did this using excavation equipment, backhoes, with a very skilled operator that we had worked with in the past, and as we scraped away the layers about ten centimetres at a time we noticed that there was definitely a grave there, the outline came through, which you can see on page 12, figure 19, which is the third image in the bottom. That's the entire process there. As -- there you go. So that is an image of when we located the grave. And you see another feature in the soil, another grey feature in the soil. That's a pre-existing trench that was -- that held a water line, that water line was severed when the trench -- when the grave was dug, and then later reconnected, which was very interesting because for us it showed that whoever reconnected that water pipe after the grave had severed it, had knowledge of the grave, since they put the new water line around it, and you can see that lower in that page, in figure 20. There is a map, a drawing showing exactly what happened. That is correct. So we found -- not only did we find the grave but we also found this pre-existing water pipe and its reconnection around the grave. After we had found the grave, then we began by removing its contents. In other words, removing the soil that had been put in, and it's a different colour, so it comes off fairly easily. I had a professor of archaeology, Professor Ochsenschlager, who said that if you ever want a leave a mark in this world, you should dig a hole, and this is exactly what happened here. The natural soil was compacted in such a way that it was fairly easy to remove the fill that was put in there on top of the bodies. As we removed the soil that was on top of the bodies, then the bodies became evident. And what was evident here was that there was -- you can see on page 13, figure 21 -- there was several concentration of bodies. We named these concentration 1, concentration 2, and concentration 3. And the reason for this was because there was gaps between these concentrations where there were no complete bodies but only body parts. This also showed us that the bodies that would have been there initially were removed and that produced truncated parts, in other words severed bodies on the edges, but also produced body parts that we found within the -- within those grave areas and nowhere else. And you can see this very clearly on page 14, figure 24. This grave had a length of 15 metres and 80 centimetres and a width of 5 metres and 80 centimetres as well, with an average depth of about 1 metre 40. It wasn't very deep but it was a very big grave. In this grave, we found 127 bodies, and then we also found two bodies that were in a nearby ditch that was probably a drainage ditch for the field. The entire field is called Lazete 1, and this is the Lazete 1 grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you uncover any evidence indicating how the grave had been dug or how it had been subsequently robbed?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, we did find tooth marks of -- machine tooth marks in the walls, and also the indication that the grave, the initial grave contours had been changed by a secondary exhumation. If you turn to page 15, you can see the location of body parts and the two robbing areas that we identified. So the two areas in orange are the areas where there were no complete bodies, all the way to the bottom, but there was presence of body parts. And also, in the grey areas that you see there, there was presence of bodies that had been severed, along the edges of the robbing areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: As well as exhuming -- excavating and exhuming the contents of each grave, did you carry out any work in the surrounding area of the field and identify any artefacts or bodies or body parts in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, initially, before we began to excavate the area, in other words to take off the top layer, we did conduct a surface search. Within this surface search, we found 456 shell cases, and they were assembled in a corner of the field. If you turn to page 10, you can see a picture and also a map of where the location of the shell cases, as well as some -- some bullets. Now, the -- this type of ballistic evidence was also found within the grave, but these were found in situ on the surface and were probably maintained there because the secondary vegetation grew around them after they were initially deposited there, and also in the ground on the track.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could just zoom in briefly on the chart in the centre right of that page, just so we can see the scale, the distances marked on there. Mr. Peccerelli, can you just describe briefly what we are seeing on this chart?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. What you can see there is the corner of the field and the distribution of the shell cases that were found. Most of them are on the side of the track. In other words, in the lower picture you could see there there is flags on the track; those flags signify the finds of those shell cases. From there to the left, going into the field. Those groupings suggested there was firing going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just so we are clear with the terminology, when you're referring to shell casings, what kind of size of weapon would fire the sorts of shell casings that you were finding?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: From the look of it, these look like 762 millimetre shell casings. What kind of weapon? A 762 rifle, a Kalashnikov, I think it's called. I'm not a weapon expert, but it's fairly simple to measure the length and also the diameter on the shell cases to be able to see. And you could also see that they were spent because they had the percussion in the bottom of the shell case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask a short question in between? Sir, you said those groupings suggested that there was firing going on there. This is page 13, line 20. What do you mean by that? And what is the foundation for -- what do you mean by "firing"? And what is the foundation of your estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because we found these in situ, located around the grave in only one specific location. If you look, they are only grouped, I believe that to be the south part of the grave, and not all around it. Yeah, that is the southern edge of Lazete 1 area. Going up around the grave, you could -- I wish I would have done that, but if you would put the grave where you see there is a line that says outline of Lazete 1, basically the shell casings were found all the way around on one side and at the bottom of the grave, not necessarily inside of it. Those shell cases in that location appear to be, from my experience in other graves of this sort, a place where shooting was going on and the shell casings were flying out of the weapons and landing in the floor and then were covered up through time. I base this on my experience, not on the fact that I'm a ballistic expert, like I told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Another question by Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a follow-up to the Presiding Judge's question, through the interpretation that I'm getting in French, I heard that shots had been exchanged, but I'm not quite sure that there was crossfire. I'm not quite sure that was what the witness meant. I was wondering whether shots had been exchanged between two groups or whether some shots had been made, just simply been made but not exchanged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, what I'm implying is shots had been fired, not that there was an exchange. If you look, there is no opposition to the pattern. It seems to be going around an area in one direction. There is no opposing pattern of ballistics on the other side. So this would be shooting at something, not necessarily fighting against something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any information about what event or events took place at this location in terms of any individuals who had been present at the time the shooting took place or any statements from any survivors?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I would have to say I don't have any knowledge of any survival -- survivors, but I was told by one of the investigators that there was a survivor who said that people were being taken to this field from the Orahovac school, that these people were lined up and they were shot there and later pushed into the grave, but you would have to refer to the investigator's statement and the witness statement; I was only told that a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about other artefacts that you identified at this location, and could I ask that we see page 23 in e-court in the English. What objects did you find in this grave apart from human remains?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, in these pictures, you can see that the two top pictures there is people's -- persons' hands tied behind their backs, and also in the bottom one you can see a ligature, wire ligature around the person's leg. Besides these ligatures, I guess, not allowing people to move, you also have in page 22, which is the previous page, we did find 89 bodies that had pieces of material around the head, in some cases around the eyes, which we named probable blindfolds. Not only did we find them on those 89 bodies but we also found, I believe, another 37 or so in the grave fill that probably fell off the other bodies. They fit the profile exactly; in other words, they're the same colour, the same scalloped edges, these were very particular pieces of cloth. If you go to page 22, you can see some of those images of the cloths that I'm referring to. You can see there -- well, on all of the images there is pieces of cloth covering sometimes the eyes and sometimes these have fallen a little lower because of decomposition and are covering either the nose or the mouth. Besides this, we also found some wrist watches and other -- I believe on three other bodies we found identification documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the pictures we are seeing now on the screen, are these pictures taken of the probable blindfolds as they were when they were uncovered by your team?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, they are. These are images taken in situ as the bodies were found, and the body number is there as well. Lazete 1, body 489, body 660, body 534, 559, 518. These were taken for several reasons. One were to document, obviously, the entire process; another reason was because during the transport to the morgue, these might have moved and we needed to make sure we were documenting exactly where we were finding these pieces of cloth systematically around these bodies' heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we go now to page 18 of the English report. It has the heading chapter XI, Body Parts, which I think may be page 28 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In your report, Mr. Peccerelli, you distinguish between bodies and body parts. What is the difference between those two categories?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, since we started work in Bosnia in 1997, we came up with this distinction because not everything, not all the bodies that we were recovering were complete. So we had to come up with the term "body part." The body part would be several bones that were articulated and they could help us identify someone. These were not just loose remains, these were actual parts of bodies, but they didn't constitute an entire body. In other words, they weren't given a body number and there is no body sheet filled out for them. They were given a log number with a BP in front of it and a picture was taken of them. But most of the body parts are important in these primary graves because they are usually located in the robbed areas. In other words, these body parts came about after the primary inhumation, or the burial of the bodies. When some of the bodies were removed, and as the forces of that removal occurred, they severed some of the parts of those bodies that were taken and some of them stayed behind. As you can see, they are different. One is a leg, and here you have a person's skull and cervical vertebrae.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the skull and cervical vertebrae, is that in the image just coming on the screen now from the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is. You can see basically a person's face there, and their neck, and you would also notice that this person has no teeth. This is interesting also because we found some dentures in the surface as well. So it's sort of different pieces of the puzzle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to Lazete 2. When did you start to work on that site?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: We began to work on Lazete 2 on August 2, about six days before we ended Lazete 1. This is because most of the team was exhuming the bodies from within grave 1, in other words Lazete 1, but I had equipment and a couple of archeologists free, and also we had conducted our work in Lazete 1 a lot faster than we anticipated, so I was asked to go and look at this field to see if there was any possibilities of exhuming a grave there since there had been some reports that in the 1996 exhumation there were some bodies left behind. So what we did is we began to do the same type of procedure; we began by stripping the surface, which took several days of preparation, so by the time we ended Lazete 1, the Lazete 2 site and the grave had been found and was ready also for exhumation and removal of its contents. So it worked out quite nicely. And also because the two sites were a couple of hundred metres away, I mean, they were walking distance from each other, just along the other side of the train tracks. So all of our equipment was already there, the right personnel wasn't busy, and we had a question, which was to look in to see if all the evidence had been recovered. When we began to do this, the first thing that occurred was that we noticed that a surface find or surface search had not been conducted in the original exhumation, so we found -- we found even more shell cases in Lazete 2 than in Lazete 1. Overall, we found 671 shell cases on the surface there. Also, this grave is a lot larger than Lazete 1, but we found in all 830 artefacts. 671 of these were shell cases, 20 live rounds, 46 bullets, and 34 strips of material, which, I should mention, the strips of material that were found in Lazete 2 were also consistent with the ones found in Lazete 1, linking in some way the two events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You've mentioned the prior excavation in 1996. Do you have any information or did you have any information at that time why Lazete 2 wasn't fully excavated in 1996?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, I think, speaking to Dr. Bill Haglund, who was in charge of the exhumation, there was security issues, where decisions had to be made as far as how much time they could spend at the site, and apparently they chose to, instead of uncovering the entire surface, they decided to trench. In other words, they put two trenches in and hit two body concentrations, so by doing this they found two large locations of bodies and I think they named these two different graves. I don't think they were concerned so much about the archaeology of the site, more about the recovery of those bodies. And that's pretty much what I know. What we discovered when we got in there was that in fact Lazete 2 was not comprised of two graves but it was one large grave. This grave was 37.70 metres in length, and about 40 -- four metres in width. It's a very large grave. It's more than twice the size of Lazete 1. You can probably appreciate the length of the grave and the size of it if you go to the cover page, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In fact, if I could ask for P939 to be put on the screen. The cover page has an image on it, if we could zoom in on that, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I think the same image is also displayed on page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think for this purpose we can just have the English up. It's just to show the picture. It would be more visible if we have it across the full width of the screen. Excuse me, Mr. Peccerelli, but if you would like to continue with that image now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Sure. Several things you would be able to see. All the way in the background, behind the de-mining vehicle you'll see there, you'll see the train tracks, also a tent which is where -- well, that's where I remained most of the time I was there. I was taking notes and directing the team. Also one of our excavators, a little backhoe that we had there. But this is very advanced in the process. We had recovered most of the fill of the grave, but you can see that the grave itself is very long. Where the backhoe is working is one of the areas where the original exhumation was conducted in 1996, where they found one of the two concentrations of bodies. Also very interesting about this site is if you look on the right of the screen, on the surface you will see a water pipe running along on top of the -- there it is -- on top of the grave. It's interesting because when they dug this grave, they also severed that water pipe. I'm guessing by mistake they just had bad luck in both fields, they hit the water pipes, and in this case as well they reconnected the water pipe around -- around the grave, again showing that they knew exactly where the grave was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you also tell us a bit about what we are seeing on the interior of the grave, particularly the sides of the, what I would say the grave wall, where we can see some marks. What do those marks represent, if anything? Why are they there?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, if you look on the left side, close to the bottom of the screen, you will see on the left side of the screen, the bottom, you will see there are three tooth marks and also a scoop. Those are imprinted in the original wall of the grave. The reason why that's there is because, again, the original natural soil has been compacted for thousands, maybe millions of years, and when you scrape into it you sort of draw a feature into the wall. Once you put the top soil mixed in there, it never will compact in the same way, so it's fairly easy to remove that top soil and then you get the natural features. This is obviously very careful excavating. We had some very proud British archeologists who had a lot of experience in these ancient type of sites and who conducted this very careful excavation of the walls. They also led us to see that. Now, if you look --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just before we continue, in fact, Mr. Peccerelli, and again while we have the image on screen where you mentioned the water pipe, I wanted to clarify, because you said that when they dug the grave, they must have had the bad luck of hitting the water pipe, or something to that effect. Who do you mean by "they"? Because we've heard from you that the grave must have been dug originally and then it was also excavated by the team led by Bill Haglund in 1996. So who is it who hit this water pipe?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, the people who originally dug the grave. In this case, the original perpetrators that dug this grave in the soil with the purpose of depositing bodies in it. Dr. Bill Haglund's team didn't do -- they did very little excavating around this area, and only dug in two areas of the whole grave. I don't think they even found this water pipe. As a matter of fact, if you go to page 16 of the same report, you can see there the differences -- there is a layout on the drawing of the entire grave whereby they -- Bill Haglund 's excavation team dug in comparison to the size of the entire grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You need to go one page further, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps go for a moment to the previous image. Judge Mindua wants to put a question to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a point of clarification. I would like to clarify something. Please correct me if I'm wrong, but I see in the actual trench, I see the soil, which is quite dark, almost black, and on the left-hand side of the screen I see some soil which is of a more greyish colour, almost purple. I was wondering why there are different colours. What is this mount of earth or soil that we see on the top left-hand corner of the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think you have to understand that this picture, there is shade over the grave so it's made to appear a little darker than it actually is. Directly over the grave. But what it is is that when -- most of the graves that we found in Bosnia, because of decomposition itself and because of the mixture of soils, tend to turn a bit darker than the rest. What you have, those mounds of dirt that are piled up on the upper left-hand corner, is the top soil that was removed from the surface to get down to this level. That top soil is of a different colour than the contents in the soil of the grave, basically because it's mixed. One is natural and the other one is a mixture of different natural soils with the decomposition from the bodies. I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does answer my question. And I see that there are three people and I was wondering what was their job, who are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's Jean Marie, Mirko, and I think Claudia. They are Guatemalan, a Canadian Chilean, and an American, part of the team. They are named in the -- in the list of people who worked in this case, and they are archeologists. Their job is to locate, excavate, and exhume the remains and the bodies that we find in these graves and also the evidence, as well as document the entire process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wonder if you could, or are you in a position to say -- can we remain on this picture, please. I think you have stated in your evidence that among the artefacts found were bullets and bullet shells. Are you in a position to say whether these bullets were fired on this site or they were -- they would have been brought from some other place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may turn to an image that will help us answer the question. If you turn to page 10, we can see the grouping of shell cases on the surface. What you see in the bottom left-hand corner is the beginning of grave Lazete 2C, which is the big grave that we are talking about. That's where, more or less, where the machine was working and the tent was. The grouping, if you notice, again, it has the same type of grouping as it did in Lazete 1, which is basically a one-sided, sort of an L-shaped, one-sided approach to the firing. These shell cases were in the ground, under secondary vegetation. Some of them buried under half a centimetre of soil. I would say that these bullet casings were there from -- for a long time, and they were not brought there. They were most likely fired at this location. And again, you could pick one up and look at the bottom and they were shot there. There was also bullets and also spent bullets, and also live shells that we found, but most of the majority, the large majority, 671 of them, were shell cases that had been fired, and they were found in this location, in this grouping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just one clarification: The position in which they are grouped is exactly the position in which they are -- in which they were fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The position which they are mapped is the location where we found them. It depends on the weapon, and here again I'm not a weapons expert, but it depends on whether the machine that is doing the firing, I guess, spills the bullet to the right, to the left, how far it shoots it, but it's a matter of a person standing there, or in other cases if the machine, the machine-gun or the rifle, whatever was used there, had a tripod, this would also have a certain pattern to how far the shell cases fall from the weapon, and for example, how many people were standing there at the time, this would create this type of pattern. So basically what you have is, as you shoot, the shell cases go flying a certain distance and fall on the ground, people step on them, they get covered and years go by. This is a mapping of where we found them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: How many bodies were found in this grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only found 16 bodies in this grave, as well as 26 body parts. Again, I'm not sure how many bodies were found and exhumed in 1996, but I know it's more than 16. What we found were the bodies that were in between the areas that were excavated in 1996 by the Physicians for Human Rights team, and also the bodies that were not taken during the robbing exercise that was conducted afterwards. So if you go to page 16, there is a drawing there that would help us to understand. This is a complex excavation because basically there was four excavations carried out at the site. The initial excavation of the site, again, placed sometime between June 5th, 1995, and June 27th, 1995. Sometime between those times which are the dates on those aerial images.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting but we are seeing on the screen a reference to July 5th and July 27th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yeah, July. July 5th, 1995, and July 27th, 1995. That's when the original grave was dug here. Later on, at a time that we don't know but after July 27th, and if we go to, let's see, Lazete 1, there is also a date for the time that the grave was expanded with the aerial images. I don't know if those aerial images exist for Lazete 2, it would have to be done, but for Lazete 1, the grave was expanded; in other words, somebody dug at this grave again between September 7th, 1995, and September 27th, 1995. So in other words, only two months after its original creation, somebody came back and they excavated in these two areas that you can see here, robbing area A and robbing area B. They took quite a few of those bodies out, and the only bodies that we recovered were the bodies that were at the very bottom, against the wall, in the edges, in other words, in the perpendicular part of the grave. Since the excavation, the machine, has a natural curve, it misses the bodies that are in the bottom, so these bodies were basically up against the wall and were missed by the robbing excavation, also in area A and area B. What you can see, those larger areas, which are LO2A and L02B, that's where the Physicians for Human Rights team excavated in 1996, so that would be the third event, those two excavations. And the fourth excavation would be the one I conducted in 2000. So this site was overall excavated four different times: Once between July 5th and July 27th, once soon after that to rob some of these bodies in areas A and B, once in 1996 by the Physicians for Human Rights team, and then finally in 2000 by the ICTY exhumation team that I led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: One further question: Who sited these graves for excavation? Like, who discovered them and then for you to be able to go there and start the excavations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the investigators of the Prosecution of ICTY. They are the ones that investigated. Dean Manning is the one that took me to the place and gave me the aerial images, and told me that they were looking for graves here and my job was to find them with those aerial images and with the information they had. I also believe they had information from a witness as well as, I'm guessing, other information that led us to these two places. But they led us to Lazete 1 initially and then Lazete 2 had been dug in 1996, so they knew of that grave, but while we were there they asked us to re-excavate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could go briefly back to the cover page, the first page image that we were looking at. Mr. Peccerelli, you mentioned the work that was being carried out by the team actually inside the grave, and I think you even made reference to some British archaeologists who were particularly careful in their work, having worked on very ancient sites. We can see some tools being used by the three members of your team working here. What are they using and what kind of process are they carrying out that we can see?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, the tools we typically use once we get down to excavating those features, or excavating the bodies, are anywhere from archaeological trowels, there are again some British trowels, and there is a lot of history in British archaeology so they have their own very developed special tools, so there are these British trowels that we love to use. We also use chopsticks. Chinese chopsticks are shaped and they are very helpful to dig around bones. And also small brushes. So usually what you would do is you would take a trowel to get at the level of the remains, then you would use one of these Chinese chopsticks to clean around very specific areas, and also this is done very carefully because sometimes we find bullets associated with the remains, or other evidence. We have to be very careful. And then, finally, you would use a brush. You see they also have pails, because the dirt that is removed immediately around the bodies is also later screened to make sure we don't miss any bone fragments or any bullets or any other type of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please can we go now to page 24, e-court page number in English, so that's, I think, page 23, according to the numbers at the bottom. And as with the Lazete 1 report, your report for Lazete 2 describes finding probable blindfolds in the grave. Can you just point out on the images captioned on this page whether there are any such artefacts; and when we are done with this page, if you would also look at the same question on the next page.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I don't know what I just did. If you look in the top picture, at the skull, you will see that there is a cloth going around it right here. That is one of those pieces of cloth that we refer to as a probable blindfold. Once again, you will see that these bodies are directly against the soil, and again you will see the difference in colour. One is because there is still a little bit of the fill, which is the grey soil, and then the natural soil is the brownish soil. As well as you'll see that this person has Wellington boots and clothing. I think in the next page, we might be able to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move from this page, Mr. Elderkin -- no, please don't move from that place -- page. Did you want the witness to mark some parts of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I just wanted to show the skull, but when I did that, the pen, the whole thing just blew up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Not specifically, Your Honour, simply for him to talk to us about what we're seeing on screen I think is clear enough on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has a question in relation to this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: In relation to this photograph at page 28, line 16, you are saying something about probable blindfolds. Can we just clarify that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lazete 2 report only has 26 pages. I'm not sure if this is referring to the first report, which is the Lazete 1 report, which has a page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If I'm correct, Your Honour, you were referring to the transcript page 28, so page 28 of what we are talking about today, not page 28 within Mr. Peccerelli's report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was in relation to this photo we have on the screen now. Could you indicate where you see a probable blindfold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. We question was to simply explain the idea of a probable blindfold as opposed to a blindfold.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Because at this time some of the cloths that were around the bodies' heads had been moved, we decided to say "probable blindfold" instead of "blindfolds," because in order to be a blindfold, it should be over the eyes. It was a matter of being exact. So we believed that although they were moved and they were somewhere along the head, this was due to the bodies being moved and decomposition, and also because there was consistency in the pieces of cloth - most of them were pink, most of them had scalloped edges - it's -- there seemed to be very systematic placement of cloths around the bodies that we found, 89 of them in Lazete 1 and I think eight in Lazete 2, as well as over 30 loose pieces of cloth found in the fill in Lazete 1 and over 30 found in the fill in Lazete 2. So there was consistency in both sites as far as the colour and the shape of these pieces of cloth as well as their location on the bodies of -- on the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Indeed, since we have discussed a little bit further the subject of these probable blindfolds, now we have the large image on screen, I at least would be grateful if, Mr. Peccerelli, you could use the electronic pen just to indicate with an arrow of the location of where you consider there to be a probable blindfold in this image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you perhaps make a slightly larger mark, please, Mr. Peccerelli, so it shows up. Am I right that then you've circled the area indicating the probable blindfold?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct. I've circled the area where you can see -- that's the skull. You can see a piece of cloth surrounding it and this is what we believe to be -- well, we know, we recovered it, this is a piece of cloth on the person's head, and we named it a probable blindfold. There was also done -- and this is going on a little bit -- because these bodies had to be transported to the morgue and we didn't want to assign a set name to these cloths that might later be changed by the -- by the morgue or the pathologist, so we wanted to make sure that it was noted that we were seeing something systematic in colour, shape, and location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might ask for the admission of this as an in-court exhibit marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked photograph will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This will be Exhibit P1439. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, since we have now spent some time with the Lazete 2 report, that was not admitted through the witness in a prior testimony but I would ask that it be admitted at this stage, and it's premarked as P939, 65 ter is 6483.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be received as an exhibit with this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if we may see the next page now in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Peccerelli, if you can briefly talk us through what we see in the images on this page, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, these images show four bodies. Three of them have -- well, actually four of them have pre-excavation fractures. Pre-excavation fractures were fractures that were found at the time of the exhumation that occurred prior to us excavating the body. Once again, this is terminology used not to come into contrast with the findings of the anthropology or pathology teams but this is what we believe to have been caused by some type of trauma, either prior or around the time of death. In three of these images, the one on the right and the two on the bottom, also show the probable blindfolds again, and always associated with the skull.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could turn now to the next page, which is titled, I think, "Isolated Artefacts" and if you could give us a brief commentary on what we are seeing on the images of that page, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: These are some of the pieces of cloth that were found isolated, in other words, not as directly associated to one of the bodies but that were consistent enough with the probable blindfolds for us to give them a specific artefact number. And we found 34 of these strips of material, and if you look at these and compare them to the ones found in Lazete 1, they are very consistent with those. You can see the scalloped edges in both and also the pink colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Lastly, if we can turn now to the last page of the report, and again if you could please comment on the artefacts shown in the photographs there.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: We also found isolated wrist watches, and we described basically what we saw. Some of these wrist watches, and this is something that we found in other sites that were excavated, that these were in some cases, at least, I know of the Seikos, these are automatic watches that basically don't need to be wound and don't need battery, they sort of wind themselves with movement. And they usually stop functioning 24 to 36 hours after movement has stopped. And in some of these cases, you can see that there is a time and also a date, and there is consistency between the dates of five of these between the 15th and the 16th. We don't know what month or if the times have anything to do with it but we figured that this consistency should be shown in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Peccerelli. I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Elderkin. Mr. Tolimir, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to welcome the witness. May God's will be done in these proceedings and not necessarily mine. And while we are looking at the sight that the witness has on his screen, could the witness please explain and tell us whether these watches have been preserved as evidence that can be used in the future? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: What I can say is that we allocated evidence numbers to this evidence. LZ02C artefact is A01, 08, 016, 388, 393, 555, 704 and 826. This evidence was handed over to Mike Hedley, who is the scene of crime officer. This evidence was later placed within the refrigerated containers and transported to Visoko and handed over to the morgue team. That's as far as I know. I would assume that this evidence is held somewhere or that it was documented enough that it would still be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If it were to be found where you left it, what information could we establish from that in order to help us to see what had happened?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, if you could look at these watches again, I mean, these wrist watches, what they will show you are times and dates, and the only thing that can be established from that was 24 to 36 hours prior to those times and those dates, the people wearing these watches stopped moving, or the watches themselves were removed from the people that were wearing them, so it would give us a time frame pretty much. That's about all you can get from these. Or, if I may add, if they have inscriptions underneath or something, that might help, but I don't recall that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, the locality where you found the watch or the two watches that we have before us, what could you establish about the locality based on the objects you found there? And what did you record based on those objects? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, the location of these objects, these two objects were within the grave in Lazete 2. The objects were photographed and they were mapped within the grave. That information would be in the -- in the registry log, in the evidence log, the exact location within the grave, but we only recovered what we found either on the surface or in the grave that was associated with this site as well as with Lazete 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for repeating my question. Your answer wasn't clear and I want to understand your answer as a lay person. What can you establish based on a watch, given the time span between 24 and 36 hours? Can you establish any information about the age of the victims, when they were buried, and so on and so forth? What could one decipher from the watches? What kind of evidence do watches make? Why did you keep the watches?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, the watches gave us one type of evidence, was a time frame. Again, some of these watches are automatic. It gave us a time frame of when either they were removed from the person who was wearing them or that the person who was wearing them stopped moving. So they would put a time frame for us of when that watch was put into that grave. It would not tell us about the age or the sex of a victim. It would tell us about when that watch was put into the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we are talking about a mass grave, Lazete 2, where these watches were found, can you tell us were you able to establish the time when the watches stopped working? What was the time, approximately, when that happened? What year? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, we could not establish what year. The watches don't have that type of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether the watches stopped working after the person wearing them stopped moving, or did the watches continue working even if the persons were no longer alive but were transported in a vehicle? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on these watches. I would have to say that I possess one myself and the person has to be moving constantly for the watches to continue working. After the 36 hours, if there is no movement, they stop. I really can't say any further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time for our first break today? I see you are in agreement with that. Sir, we must have our first break today and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break, we were talking about these watches that we can see on our screens. There is something else I would like to know: What was the established practice, given what you told us? Would these be kept throughout the procedure or would they be destroyed once the forensic people had had a look as well as the anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I will have to say that I'm not aware of where these watches would be now, but it -- normally, any type of evidence would -- should be kept until the proceedings are done, but I'm not sure what ICTY rules state about evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Before we move on to any other issues, can we please go back to the blindfolds. We talked about that before the watches. You were asked questions by the Judges about the alleged blindfolds. The alleged blindfolds, or probable blindfolds, and blindfolds as such . What is the distinction between the two? Did you find -- what I mean to ask you is this: Did you find a single blindfold that was actually on a body covering the eyes, in other words precisely where it was meant to be, or were all of the ones that you found simply alleged or probable blindfolds?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, we did find many that were covering the eyes. I can't give you the exact number, I would have to go case-by-case to look at that number, but in some of the cases they had lowered or gone higher, but in quite a few of the cases, as a matter of fact, if we may, I think in the Lazete 1 report, page 22, you can clearly see that there are one, two, three, four, five, six, seven at least that are over the eyes, on page 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, and excuse me, General Tolimir. I'm not sure everyone has the hard copy of the report, so if you wanted to see it on screen, it's P935 for the Lazete 1 report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was also just looking for the P number of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So you can clearly see on these images that the first two in the left in the top row, as well as the second one, the one on the right in the second row, the one in the middle on the third row, and the two on the right in the bottom row, they all have their eyes covered with these probable blindfolds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Probable blindfolds or blindfolds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blindfolds if you like to -- these are directly over the eyes, yes, blindfolds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peccerelli. This is on page 3, line 4, of the transcript, you spoke about the probable blindfolds and blindfolds, and then I wrote this down: Location 89, eight of those were found in one place, 30 in another place. I didn't mean to ask you a trick question, I simply wanted to know. Thank you for your answer and thank you for clarifying that, sir. My next question: Page 27, lines 11 through 18 of the transcript, there and before that, you talked about how the exhumations started on the 5th of June, 1995, in that location and continued until the 27th of June, and then the Medecins Sans Frontieres [as interpreted] were there and they were followed by an ICTY team in 2006. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The dates are wrong. What I meant was that we have images, aerial images, that show no disturbance on the field on July 5th of 1995 and then disturbance on the field of -- on the 27th of July of 1995. The PHR team, which is Physicians for Human Rights, worked in 1996, and later I worked at that same site in the year 2000. This is referring to Lazete 2 site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that and stating the exact dates. The Medecins Sans Frontieres [as interpreted] worked there in 1995, and you only came five years later, in 2000. In that case, my question would be: Did you notice any alterations to that location, Lazete 2, anything that might have affected the possibility of ascertaining facts and collecting evidence due to these alterations or any modifications to the site?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, and again excuse me. I'm seeing references twice now to Medecins Sans Frontieres, and although it's not a huge misstatement, it's perhaps simply an interpretation issue, I think for keeping the record clear and being able to find references later on, it would help if we have the reference to Physicians for Human Rights in place of those two references, which are at page 38, line 18, and page 39, line 2, of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, I was wondering myself how it came that you were referring to Medecins Sans Frontieres. Perhaps it was just a --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. For the sake of the transcript I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You spoke about the Physicians for Human Rights. The Physicians for Human Rights worked there in 1996, and then in the same location where you worked there were representatives of the people from the International Tribunal in 2000. Four years later, were any changes noticed at the location that significantly altered the site, thereby making it impossible to ascertain any facts or indeed to obtain evidence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: When we got there, there was no visible notice of any alterations to the site. And this was because when Physicians for Human Rights worked in 1996, they did not do a surface recovery that allowed us to recover all the surface finds, including the bullet casings and bullets that were still on the surface. However, there was change to two areas of the grave, which you can see on page 16 of the Lazete 2 report. The two areas where Physicians for Human Rights dug were excavated beyond the original limits of the grave, thereby changing the shape of the grave only in those two areas, and that was mapped out and you can see it on that image. The two areas that are larger are the two areas excavated by Physicians for Human Rights, which are the ones labelled in the bottom LZ02A and LZ02B. Those are the two areas where Physicians for Human Rights excavated. The two areas called "robbing area A" and "robbing area B," or in the bottom, LZ02C and LZ02C, those two areas Physicians for Human Rights did not excavate. They missed it altogether. They didn't touch those two areas. In other words, they did not change the areas because they were not excavated at the time, and in those locations, that's where we found the 16 bodies and the 26 body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At the very beginning, Mr. Elderkin asked you a question and you responded at line 8, or rather, page 8 of today's transcript, line 22. You spoke about information, DNA information, provided by the victims' families. My question: Can you tell us which relatives were the DNA samples taken from that were used to identify the victims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I had no involvement with the DNA identification operation in these cases. I was specifying my experience in Guatemala and in the cases in Guatemala. In those cases you would usually take samples from the parents and the children, and if you don't have parent or children, then you go to siblings. But I'm not sure of how the testing was done in -- to identify these victims. I'm sure the people conducting the identifications at ICMP can provide that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for this explanation, sir. In Guatemala can more distant relatives be used, someone who is not a sibling, a father, or a child to successfully ascertain the identity of a victim? For example, a relatively close relative provides a DNA sample without necessarily being a brother, a father, or a child. In other words, a relative twice removed, for example. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: There is nothing impeding that a far removed relative be used other than the fact that the further the relationship, the blood relationship or the genetic relationship is, the more difficult it would be to prove the identification of the individual statistically. In other words, it has to do with how different that person is from the population and how close that person is from that specific relative. It's difficult to generalise and each case should be looked at individually. It can be done but it is more difficult than if you have parents, children, or siblings, but we have used grandparents, uncles and aunts, and nieces and nephews, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an expert, what about this: If we take a DNA sample from a father, so the genetic material comes 50 per cent from the father and 50 per cent from the mother. If that is the case, what about the decreasing percentage in a brother or a sister or an aunt or an uncle? Even less. And then even less from a more distant relative. Can you explain the limits of that approach, in terms of ascertaining kinship or, rather, in terms of using a DNA sample from a relative like that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Like I mentioned to you earlier, not only do you have to contemplate the relationship - and you are correct, when we look at nuclear DNA, we are talking about 50 per cent coming from the mother and 50 per cent coming from the father - but we also have two other types of DNA that we can look at, which are mitochondrial DNA, which comes from the maternal line, and Y chromosome DNA, which comes from the paternal line. With the combination of the different tests, and depending on the differences of the individuals with the population, this can increase the possibility of identification. Now, again, I also did mention earlier that we don't work with DNA in an isolated environment. We were also relying on ante-mortem information, also on information that comes from the exhumation site, and also on information that comes from the anthropological analysis. So DNA on its own is not being used but it's a combination, it's another tool to try to reach an identification. Obviously you are right: The further you get, the less possibility of identifying someone; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So the possibility decreases for a chromosome overlap in the case of a distant relative and the more difficult it becomes to identify a victim because of the distance of this relation. Would that be a fair statement, sir? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, it would. I would have to agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief, you said that in 2000, you were, as far as I understood, the deputy manager for that archaeological team, as you called it. You said you worked with Professor Richard Wright's team. Is my understanding correct? Were you the deputy head of that team in 2000? And did you work with Richard Wright? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I had worked under Richard Wright during the 1997 exhumations and also during the 1998 exhumations. He had to go back to Australia for two or three months during the 2000 field season, and he contacted me and asked me if I would accept a deputy position under him so that he may absent himself and that I would take over during his absence. So I accepted. He -- we saw each other when I got there, he handed over the team and the exhumation agenda, and then when he came back, I handed it back to him. And as a result, I was responsible for the exhumation of Lazete 1 and Lazete 2 in its completeness, so I did these two cases in Richard Wright's absence, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for this explanation. I asked that because Richard Wright appeared in this trial as a witness. In Professor Richard Wright's absence, you headed that team, that's what my question was about, during your work at Lazete 1 and Lazete 2. Am I right, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given this question and given all the other questions, could you please describe the following: How did that team operate in terms of responsibility within the team? That's what I need to know for the time being, thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, the archaeology team was headed by me. I took the decisions. Under me, I would assign a person that would coordinate the exhumation during the grave, and we might call this a pit boss. Basically an exhumation coordinator. And then we also had the rest of the archeologists. What I did is I named a different exhumation coordinator every week to give everyone the opportunity to oversee that part of the procedure. We also had a surveying archaeologist, a photographer, and a team of scene of crime officers as well as a de-mining team, security officers, and we were accompanied by, in this case, by US army personnel that provided security for us. There was also a logistic team that provided logistics as far as the trucks and drivers and that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us about the structure of this team, no specific persons involved. Could you tell us who you were subordinate to. Who was your boss and who did you report to? Who did you submit requests to, to use our own military language? I hope you understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember his name. I think it was Strongman was his last name. He was what we called India Charlie 1, so he was in charge of the entire operation. And I reported to him on general issues, but on technical aspects I didn't report to anyone. I was the person leading the methodological approach and the scientific approach to the investigation at these sites. I also coordinated with the investigating -- with the investigators of the ICTY, and once in a while would also talk by phone, by satellite phone, to The Hague, also to investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tolimir, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need a clarification, and if I've got my facts wrong, please let me know. I don't have a specific reference so if I caught you wrong, again you should let me know. You have said that the first exhumation started somewhere in June 1996 and this was done by Physicians for Human Rights. Your own exhumation started in 2000; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Right. During that period between PHR and your own exhumation, how was the site secured, say from vandalism or abuse or intrusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are talking about Lazete 2, because Lazete 1, which was the site that I went to, was never excavated before. When I found the site, it wasn't necessarily being protected other than immediately around the time that we were going to get there, that we were going to work there. Lazete 2 was also a field that I'm not sure, I really don't know if it was protected from 1996 to 2000. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. In relation to the previous question, if you remember, to the extent that I could understand, you said that there was this person called Strongman to whom you submitted your general reports. Could you tell us what his capacity was? Within your team, in relation to this International Tribunal, what was his position? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Brian Strongman was his name. I remember now. I think Brian Strongman was the leader of the team in the field in general. I'm not sure of his mandate specifically but we basically communicated continuously.
