He was in charge of, more than anything, of meeting with military officials to coordinate security, as well as communicating here with The Hague, and also having to do with work-related issues, and contract-related issues. I was in charge of the methodological side of things and the scientific side of things, but I understood that there was a hierarchy and he was, to my understanding, immediately above me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What about Mr. Brian, who you just told us about, Strongman. Could he give you any instructions, could he advise you, could he order you anything to do in relation to anything to do with your work or the work of your team? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: More than anything on security issues and, as far as times had to do, like which site to do first or second. But as far as how to go about the work itself, no, he could not advise me. Mr. Brian Strongman, if I'm not mistaken, was a retired policeman from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was his position in your team, in terms of hierarchy? What was the name of that position? You have just told us what his authorities and competences were, but what was the title of his position in the team?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I will have to say maybe team leader. I really don't know. I can't really remember. It wasn't an issue with us. It was -- he was there more permanently than I was, so he was there for the entire season and I came and took over the technical lead while Richard went back to Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have also told us that you maintained coordination with representatives of the ICTY, primarily those who were in the field as well as those who were here in The Hague, but I didn't understand whether your coordination was with the OTP or somebody else. Could you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, the coordination was specifically with the investigators, most of the time with Dean Manning, which was one of the investigators. Sometimes he was in Bosnia, sometimes he was here. So that's who I coordinated with most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What about others in the International Criminal Tribunal? Were you in contact with any other investigators or prosecutors here?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Not during the 2000 season, no. We were very isolated when we were in the field, and I only led the team for two and a half months, so during those two and a half months there wasn't really anything other than the normal work which was basically focused on these two sites. And work went quite well, and speedingly, so there wasn't really a need for much communication outside of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, did anybody make any changes or adjustments to the information you obtained from localities 1 and 2 in order to adapt them to locality 3? Did anybody change anything in the findings of Professor Wright with regard to the exhumations that he performed?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I guess I will try to answer the first part. I only worked at locality 1, which would be Lazete 1 and Lazete 2, and as far as I know, my report is here and I haven't seen any changes made to that. I have not seen or read Professor Richard Wright's reports and I don't know if anyone made any changes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the Court please produce Exhibit P939, page 7. Both in Serbian and in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a report from Lazete 2. We already saw this image during the examination-in-chief. And now we can see the part that I'm interested in in your report. Could we please look at page 7 in Serbian and English. Actually, we already see the relevant pages. We are looking at chapter V, where it says Exhumation Procedures. You say here Richard Wright described a general exhumation procedure as the basic instruction for the exhumation of bodies, parts of the bodies, and other evidence when exhumations were done for the International Criminal Tribunal. I have changed this general exhumation procedure and I adapted that procedure to the particular location, and an example of that general procedure was given to every archaeologist and anthropologist before they started working on exhumations. That would be my quote about the changes done to the exhumation procedures that were done at Lazete 2. Which exhumation protocol provided by Professor Wright was partly adapted in order to suit the location Lazete 2, and why those changes were made? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, this is a standard document that Richard -- Professor Richard Wright came up with in 1997. It was adapted to every single site. Sometimes only in the order of things and sometimes in who was responsible for things. In this case, if I remember correctly, the changes were probably made to the area where the exhumation supervisor was the one that had to oversee the recovery of every one of the bodies. But basically the document stayed the same throughout most of the time that we worked in Bosnia. If there were changes, they were very site-specific and very small. Small changes, such as changing the name of the site, for example, as you can see, this would be general procedures for exhumation at Lazete 2. So you had to change the name every time to Lazete 2, Lazete 1, or whichever site we were working. Sometimes the exhumation supervisor had duties inside the grave, sometimes outside the grave, but most of the procedures were basically the same, which was to make sure that we recover all the evidence and document it in every way, and this was given to everyone that worked in the field so we knew that everyone understood the instructions clearly. For example, in number 12, each shell collected had to be surveyed until a total of 10, for example, had been so recorded. That's in number 12. That -- in some cases we recorded every single one, but in these two cases there were so many that we only wanted to record 10 at that level, otherwise it would slow us down too much, so we recorded all of them in the log but we didn't necessarily take a point of all of them or photograph them all. For example, we recovered them and assigned a site description, location, and they were put in the log, everything was put in the log. So that's an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you inform the person with whom you coordinated, I believe that his name was Dean Manning, about the changes that you had made to the protocol, and what was his position with this regard, with regard to -- with regard to your changes?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No. We didn't inform him. This was an internal document that was applied to the exhumation team only and its members, so I was heading the team and it had to do with the people that supported the team, the archeologists and the anthropologists who were working there. The decision was made to do things in this manner and we did not inform, but nonetheless it's put in the report because of that reason, because these are the procedures, the mandate -- that mandated the methodology at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce page 9 in the same exhibit, P939. Again, we are talking about the same report, about Lazete 1 mass grave. Thank you. Could the Court please produce P935. This is a report about Lazete 1 mass grave. Thank you. Now we have Lazete 1. Could the Court please produce page 9 in Serbian and page 7 in English. Thank you. This has been produced and I'm going to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say here, "Bodies --" I'm reading the second bullet point in the middle. "Bodies coded in the log by the prefix B, and these include complete and truncated bodies." And after that, you say, in bullet point 3, "Body parts. Body parts coded in the logbook by prefix BP, and these include body parts and bones that were placed inside body bags and given a body part number." I suppose that they were marked. In order for everybody to understand what you're talking about, could you please make a distinction between a whole body, a truncated body, and body parts. We are particularly interested in body parts as opposed to truncated body. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: A truncated body was a body that was section cut or a part of it was displaced during a robbing operation. In other words, that we believed that the body, when put in the grave, was whole or partly whole, and this truncation occurred during a subsequent operation. A body part would be the result of that truncation. In other words, for example, you might have a body whose left lower leg was truncated. The left lower leg would be the body part. This process usually occurred during the re-excavation of the graves to remove the bodies from them. Since that wasn't done very carefully, what it produced was it produced machinery cutting through bodies, creating bodies that were truncated and also creating body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the difference between an incomplete body and body parts? What would be the criterion applied in order to establish that difference? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: We didn't really use incomplete bodies. Basically we used bodies and body parts. Because, I mean, completeness would mean 100 per cent and a lot of times we didn't have bones of the fingers, things of that sort. So for us a body was one that was there in more than 50 per cent of its original aspect and that would give us information as to the identification, as far as individualisation of that body; sex, age, stature, maybe cause of death. Body parts, on the other hand, were sometimes bones that were still articulated but that provided very little information, such as a lower limb, for example, a lower leg, a forearm, a hand. Sometimes they provided a lot of information, such as a skull and cervical vertebrae, but they were not a complete body. This is important later to also determine the minimum number of individuals. We can't assign body numbers to everything we find, and basically the difference was if it was 50 per cent or more, it was a body; if it was less than that, it was a body part. If it was a loose bone, then that would be put into a loose bone bag and that loose bone bag would later be assigned a body part number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, based on just one body part or one bone, for example, could you identify a victim or not? Are there such bones which can determine the identity of a person?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: For example, if we have -- a femur can give us information as far as the height of a person, the sex of a person, the age of a person, and it can also give us genetic information, so that would be a good example of one specific bone that provides a lot of information. The same might be said also for a hip bone or even an maxilla on the skull. It depends on the bone, it also depends on the age of the person, but that's something that is determined during the analysis of the remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you have just told us that 50 per cent of a body was considered the entire body, my question is this: If 50 per cent of a body was complete, or even more than 50 per cent there, did you assign that body a number or a code? In other words, did a body have to be complete in order to be assigned a number or a code?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: A body had to be recognised as its own entity in order not to duplicate numbers. So, for example, if you had a lower half of a body, and an upper half of a body next to each other, you will have to make sure that they didn't belong to the same body, but, yes, once we assigned that this body was an individual entity in itself, we assigned a number and we also filled out a body sheet. You can see the body sheets here in the report, in page 19 of the Lazete 1 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your explanation that you've just provided, am I right in thinking that if there was just one bone, for example, that could provide identification information, did you assign a number to that bone as a body part or as an entire body? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: If it was just a single bone, we did neither. We put it in a loose bone bag and that whole bone bag was assigned a body part number. So you might have -- we didn't in these cases but in other cases you might have 15 femurs, ten humerus, et cetera, in one bone bag, and that whole bag was then assigned a body part number. When these remains got to the morgue, then this was analysed and a minimum number of individuals was determined based on a counting of thirds of the bone that appeared the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to the bones that provided the information for identification, were those the only ones that were taken into account for identifications? As opposed to any other body parts that were recovered from the same mass grave.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say that I did not participate in the analysis of these remains, and that's a question that would have to be posed to the anthropology team or the pathology team in the morgue in Visoko. My mandate here stated that I recover the bodies and document them only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So are you in a position to tell us which bones can be used to identify a person or not? Can you tell us that, based on the experience that you gained while working on those exhumations?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Of course. Almost any bone can be used to identify someone, as long as you use a multi-disciplinary approach. Again, looking at the context, trying to understand who the victims were, getting the osteological analysis, and then if you have the possibility of DNA, then we bring all of those together. And the best example is the World Trade Centre. In the World Trade Centre, they identified victims with bone fragments the size of rice, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a document in front of us, P935. Could I please see page 9 in Serbian and page 8 in English. Thank you. I'm interested in paragraph 5 in the Serbian-language version. Page 12 in Serbian, thank you, yes, thank you, that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here you speak about the general procedure for ICTY exhumations at Lazete 1. We are interested in paragraph 5, where you say, "The scene of crime officer shall assign a number to each item of evidence." Including materials relevant for the identification of perpetrators. That's the penultimate bullet point in your report. And finally you say, "The elucidation of other matters relevant to the investigation." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question based on what you have written in here is this: Could you please explain what kind of evidence is relevant for the identification of perpetrators which you could recover from the mass graves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, in the case of these two sites, I would consider the ballistic evidence evidence that could be traced back to the perpetrators, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us more about the ballistic evidence that you use in your capacity as expert in order to identify perpetrators as you explain here in this document.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I'm not a ballistics expert. My job here was to recover all of the evidence that could later be used by other experts or the investigators. From my experience, I know that there are tool marks left on bullets and also bullet casings that can be used, but I don't know if that evidence was used or not. And it wasn't my place to use it, only to recover it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please tell us whether experts such as ballistic experts requested from you to find something in the locality that they could use to determine the distance from which fires had been shot, the type of weapons, and any other such thing that they might have used in order to establish the cause of death? For example, the distance from which shots had been fired.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: You would establish a cause of death through an analysis of the remains. I was only instructed to recover the remains and the evidence around it. As far as distance, it's something that you also might be able to see through the analysis of the remains, but you have to take into consideration things like the types of weapons that were used, which in these cases can probably be -- information can be gathered from the ballistic evidence itself. In other words, from the bullets and the bullet casings. Once again, I was in charge of the recovery effort of the remains and the evidence, not of the analysis part that came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question, based on what you have just told us, is this: How did you secure the evidence relevant for the investigation? Because this is exactly what you said, finding evidence relevant for the investigation.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Once again, this evidence was handled by the scene of crime officer. In this case Mike Hedley was the person in charge. This evidence was mapped, in some cases photographed, it was entered into the log where it was described, it was then bagged, tagged, and then transported to the morgue. At the morgue it was analysed, and I'm not sure what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. When a body is identified based on DNA samples is there any other type of relevant evidence that is gathered in order to have this identification, in order to identify the perpetrator, and in order to identify any other issues that might prove relevant in the course of investigation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I did not participate in the identification process of these bodies, so I don't know what they did as far as gathering other information that would single out perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If, for example, we only had information about an identification based on DNA samples, if there was no other information derived from the site at which a victim was found, would that affect the quality of a report such as your expert opinion, sir, the report that we have before us? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Let me read the question again, please. Well, no. In this case, the lack of or amount of information does not affect the report in any way because we are reporting on a very clear mandate; that was to look for a grave, excavate its contents, recover the bodies, exhume the bodies, recover all the evidence that was there, as part of a larger investigation. What, in the end, is found has no bearing on the quality of the report itself. We are simply reporting on what we found and, again, that information is later used by other investigators to come up with conclusions or lead their investigation in one way or another. And I'm sure it was also put together and used with other information such as witnesses or any other information they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Most of the identifications these days are done based on DNA analysis. Should these reports not include other types of information too, such as the elements provided in your report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I think it's a matter of structure. In our case, we were instructed to report on specific procedures, as far as recovery. Then I'm sure there was specific reports as far as the anthropological and pathological analysis and pathology analysis of the remains, and if that led to identifications or not, I don't know, but from my understanding, the identifications came at a later time, so it would be very difficult to include all of the information in those reports. It all depends on the setting and the case. Ideally, yes, you would want to have a report that is multi-disciplinary in approach, but that's not always the case and it doesn't have any bearing on the quality of the identifications in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us the following, please: Since there was quite a number of bodies that were found that were in pieces, mere body parts, and given the fact that the victims' DNA is used to identify the bodies, during your work at these locations, Lazete 1 and Lazete 2, were any records kept that would make it possible for the morgue personnel later on to clearly identify which part of the grave site a certain item or body were found at so that they might be able to identify the remaining parts of a body during the identification procedure? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. That information is put in the evidence log. All bodies and body parts had pictures and locations included, as far as -- and also descriptions where they were found and what they comprised of. So that information is available, and was available to the morgue, and when we transported all the evidence, we also transported a copy of that log, so they wouldn't necessarily have to ask us, they would -- the log would accompany the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another thing: What about the copies of those logs or diaries? Are copies in possession of the OTP or can they only be found wherever they happened to be kept by those carrying out the actual identification work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Office of the Prosecutor does have copies of those logs, but you would have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peccerelli, for providing all these explanations. Perhaps some of the questions were ridiculous to you, but I'm asking these questions from the perspective of my familiarity and knowledge. I thank you very much for coming. This concludes my cross-examination. You have been a great help to me in understanding certain technicalities that I had not previously understood. You are, after all, an expert. Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much, this completes my cross-examination. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with permission, yes, very briefly, and it arises out of the questioning particularly at pages 52 through 54 of the transcript, concerning the identification of particular bones and their use in counting how many victims there might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, are you familiar with the calculation that's often described as minimum number of individuals calculation?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you ever asked to calculate the minimum number of individual victims in either of the Lazete graves?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I was not. That was a job or the mandate of the morgue and the pathologists and anthropologists, specifically the anthropologists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This exceeds the scope of my cross-examination. The witness Baraybar addressed this and I think you too will easily remember this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you look at page 53, lines 19 through 54 line 1, there was a reference to the work, and I quote: "We didn't in these cases but in other cases you might have 15 femurs, ten humerus, et cetera, in one bone bag, and that whole bag was then assigned a body part number, and these remains got to the morgue and this was analysed and a minimum number of individuals was determined based on a counting of thirds of the bone that appeared the most." I think this is a clear reference and has to do something with the questioning of Mr. Elderkin. Please carry on, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, would the designation of human remains as being a body or a body part or a truncated body at the exhumation site have any impact on any later calculation of minimum number of individuals?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: None whatsoever. Once again, each one of the parts has to be counted independently of how they were labelled in the field. So it's independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And that's all I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Peccerelli, this concludes your examination today, and in this case. Thank you very much that you were able to come to The Hague again and to provide us with your knowledge. That was of great assistance. Thank you very much. And now you are free to return to your normal activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the Court Usher will assist you to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Mr. Vanderpuye will be taking the next witness, I wondered if I may be excused now from the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may continue your work in your office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, welcome to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon, Mr. President, everyone. I think we are prepared to proceed with the next witness, who I think is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. You are welcome. Would you please read aloud the affirmation of the declaration on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor, Mr. Vanderpuye, has some questions for you in the examination-in-chief. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and again good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Lazarevic. Before we get started, I just wanted to remind you - I know you've been here before - just to speak a little bit slower than you normally would in order to give the interpreters an opportunity to translate everything that you say accurately to all of us here in the courtroom. And if there is anything that I ask you that's not clear, just let me know and I'll do my best to rephrase it in a way that we can better understand one another. Let me start by asking you, do you recall having testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. on the 26th and 27th of June of 2007?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review the entirety of your testimony before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was your testimony read back to you or did you listen to an audio recording of it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I listened to an audio recording of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, having listened to your testimony, does your testimony fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today and if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to move into evidence the witness's previous testimony. That will be 65 ter 06625, that would be the under-seal version. And the public version of that testimony is 06626.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received, the first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first one will be Exhibit P1440, and the second one with the 65 ter number 06626 will be Exhibit P1441. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a brief summary of the witness's prior testimony that I'd like to read into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the time of his June 2007 testimony in the Popovic case, Mitar Lazarevic was employed as a customs official in Tuzla. He completed vocational college and trained as a teacher and he completed his national military service with the former JNA in 1979. Mr. Lazarevic was mobilised on 20 May 1992 and assigned to the Kiseljak Battalion. The battalion was later divided into two units and Mr. Lazarevic remained with the unit headquartered in the village of Malesici. This became the 2nd Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. Until his demobilisation in February 1996, Mr. Lazarevic was involved in monitoring the 2nd Battalion's registers, personnel rosters, and payroll activities. As the general services officer in the battalion command, Mr. Lazarevic reported to the battalion commander, Srecko Acimovic. Mr. Lazarevic testified that in July of 1995, around the time of the Srebrenica operations, the Zvornik Brigade command placed the battalion on alert. As such, the battalion had to be present on the lines with 100 per cent strength. Mr. Lazarevic recalled that during this period, sometime after 12 July 1995, commander Acimovic went home one day to freshen up. He returned later and informed the members of the battalion command that prisoners had been brought to the Rocevic school earlier. Acimovic said that he learned of their presence in the school from his parents and then went over to the school to investigate. There he found several soldiers, not members of the 2nd Battalion, guarding the prisoners. Acimovic recounted that the gym of the school was full with prisoners but that he did not know how many were there. He said that a few prisoners had been killed and that a local woman had been wounded in the village of Rocevic. Acimovic claimed that his demands for information from these unknown soldiers were rebuffed and then he sought to contact the Zvornik Brigade commander, Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, or his Chief of Staff, Major Dragan Obrenovic, for information at the brigade command. However, they were not available. When he called back, Acimovic spoke with whom he described as a security officer from the corps, who assured him that the prisoners were going to be exchanged the following day. Later that night, sometime between midnight and 2.00 a.m., the battalion received a coded telegram from the Zvornik Brigade command. Mr. Lazarevic did not recall who in the battalion command received the telegram but noted that it was recorded in the communications logbook. Members of the communications unit had to be called in to decode the telegram, which, as it turned out, was an order to the 2nd Battalion command to provide personnel for an execution squad to kill prisoners held at the Rocevic school. Commander Acimovic was alerted and decided that the battalion would refuse to implement the order. He then sent a telegram in reply to the brigade command to that effect. Later, Acimovic received a telephone call from the brigade command. Mr. Lazarevic and other members of the battalion command overheard Acimovic arguing about the order. In a heated and loud quarrel, he asserted that the battalion would not comply with the order. Following this call, Acimovic called in the battalion infantry company commanders, informed them about the situation, and instructed them that if directly approached by brigade personnel, not to supply any men for the planned executions. Later that morning, Acimovic went to the Rocevic school. When he returned, Acimovic told the members of the battalion command, including Mr. Lazarevic, that he had encountered a high-ranking security officer from the corps there who threatened him with a court-martial as did he not want to supply the men for the execution squad. Mr. Lazarevic did not travel to the school; however, rumours soon surfaced that the prisoners detained there were, in fact, transported to Kozluk, where they were executed. Mr. Lazarevic testified that at least two soldiers previously assigned to the 2nd Battalion were directly involved in the transport of these prisoners to the execution site. Your Honours that concludes my summary. And I do have a few follow-up questions for Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I want to just start off with a few basic questions. First, can you tell us about how far the command in Malesici is from the elementary school in Rocevic, just approximately?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Between 15 and 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how long would it take you to drive there on an average day? Just an approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Depends on what means of transportation you're using.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's just say in a car or a truck. How long would it --

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By car, you go to Malesici, and the hillside was a dirt track and you would normally take between half an hour and 40 minutes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately how far the battalion command is from Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Five or six kilometres, probably, up to seven or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a photograph. It's P94, 00094. And we'll need to go to page 190. All right. Do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is the elementary school in Rocevici, the school that I went to, meaning I was a student there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you were a student there, was it basically as it appears in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's probably been spruced up since. It wasn't like that way back when, but the outline of the building is still the same, at least as far as I can tell. Some annexes may have been built on the opposite side of the building, but seen from the road, it looks roughly like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And from this particular vantage point, are you able to see a gym that is attached to the school or near the school?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This part of the wall, I think, is the gym, to the right of our screens. I'm not positive but that's what I think it is. Towards the corner of the building and then the -- right behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the right-hand of -- very far right-hand side of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The right-hand side of my screen, you can see just under the roof a piece of the building, a section of the building, and I think that's the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to -- well, it's already in evidence, isn't it? I'd like to move to another photograph then, that's at page 191.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what we have in the frame now, this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a frontal view of the school building. To the left we can see the gym, across the playground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is the gym the smaller structure? There are two structures, I should say, on the left-hand side of the photograph. One is taller and one is shorter. Can you tell us which one of these is the gym?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The bigger one is the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us what the smaller part of it is?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Probably, but I never actually went in there. I suppose that it's probably the changing room or the locker room. That's where kids change their clothes before they take a gym lesson, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to go to a different area, and I see we have about a minute before the break, so I think this might be a good time to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we should have our second break now and we will resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, based on your prior testimony, you indicated that you did not go to the Rocevic school during the period of time that the prisoners were there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you go there subsequently? Did you go there after the prisoners had already been removed and executed?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that -- and this is at page 13367 of the transcript of -- you mentioned that your commander, Srecko Acimovic, told you, or mentioned to the brigade command, that when he went to the school, the gym was full. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And he also mentioned that there were some dead people there when he went there that first day. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you learn where these dead people were, whereabouts in the school area they were, from Commander Acimovic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The commander said that they were behind the school, and I really wouldn't be able to tell you in what direction. I can only tell you what I heard from him. I did not see any of that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that. Based on the two photographs that I showed you earlier, those were P94 pages 190 and 191, the two photographs of the school, can you tell us, when you say that they were behind the school, do you mean the side where the basketball court was, where it's the cement, or the other side of the school where we can see the grass in the photograph? If you want, I can put them back on the screen so you can take a look.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to show it again. They were in the area where grass is growing, not where the basketball court is. He said then that they were behind the gym, and the grassy area is behind the gym, so it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you about how many dead he saw?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He said a couple, a few bodies. He said that there were a couple, several. How many I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And just so we are clear for the record, is it the case that the dead people that he was talking about were, in fact, the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that how you understood?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you learn at any point, from your commander, about how many prisoners there were in the school or in the gym altogether?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was not in a position to know that. Nobody counted head. He only said that the gym was full. Nobody ever knew how many exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you whether the prisoners at the school or in the gym were soldiers or civilians or a mix of both? Did he tell you anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. However, I believe that they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that based on something that you heard from somebody other than your commander or other information that you have?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I heard from the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he tell you at any point where these prisoners had come from?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned, at page 13367 of your testimony, about -- you mentioned a woman that had been injured during the period of time that the prisoners had been detained at the school. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I remember, and that was a woman from the neighbourhood. I suppose that she was injured when shots were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you learn that also from your commander or did you hear that some place else, or from someone else?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From the commander again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you learn the name of this woman who was injured?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know her name. I know her husband. Her husband had been mobilised and he was on the same line, but I don't know the woman's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what's the name of her husband?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Petko Tanackovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that she was injured by gunfire; in other words, that she was shot?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was not my conclusion. In the evening when the commander came, he told us when shots had been fired, that woman was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you who was responsible for this shooting or --

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The same men who had escorted the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the men that escorted the prisoners, are these the same men that the commander encountered when he went to the school, as he related that to you, at the brigade -- I'm sorry, at the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were these members of the 2nd Battalion or members of another unit?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. According to him, he didn't know any of them. Apparently, they were not from our area, they were not locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you or the command have any information that members of the battalion were at the Rocevic school on the day that the commander first went there and reported to you that there were prisoners being held in and around the school?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the evening, when he returned to the battalion command, we learned from him that there were prisoners in the gym of the Rocevici school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were any members of the 2nd Battalion, to your knowledge, assigned to the school or at the school at that time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little bit about a conversation that was related to you, that your commander had with someone whom he described as a security officer from the corps. Do you remember testifying about that? This is at page 13373 of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what he told you about this conversation he had with the security officer? This is on the first day that he went to the school.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean "the first day"? Are you referring to the day when he first saw the prisoners or the second day? Because on the first day, he didn't meet with any officers, just the foot soldiers. That was on the evening when those prisoners had been brought in. On the second day, he had an argument with that officer and the other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. I'm referring to a phone call, I think it was a telephone call, that you testified to in the Popovic case, where you said that he -- he reported that he spoke to somebody that was a security officer. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I remember, but your question is probably not phrased well, or maybe I didn't understand you. During the night, he had an argument with a security officer and he said that he would not assign any of his men for that purpose, for that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I can make it a little bit clearer, my question. And we'll talk about this conversation as well. But you mentioned that the commander told you that he called the brigade command. This is on the day that he learned that there were prisoners in the school. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that you mentioned that he tried to speak to the commander of the brigade, Pandurevic, Vinko Pandurevic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I understand now. Now I understand what you asked me before. He did call somebody in the brigade and he told them that there were people in the Rocevic school that were behaving strangely, and that security officer promised him that on the following day those men would be exchanged. I didn't understand your question the first time around. So in that conversation, the commander was told that those prisoners would be exchanged the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he ever mention to you whom this security person from the corps was that he spoke to that promised him or told him that the prisoners would be exchanged the following day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. He said that it was a high-ranking officer who talked about the exchange. He never mentioned any names. I said it before that my commander, Srecko Acimovic, is a man of very few words. I did not specifically ask him, he didn't volunteer any information, so we did not talk much about the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you at the time familiar with the -- well, first let me ask you this, because I think I need to clarify it. This person from the corps, the security officer from the corps, that he referred to, can you just tell us what corps we are talking about, just so the record is clear?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that the corps to which the Zvornik Brigade was subordinate?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the members of the security organ of the Drina Corps back in July 1995, when your commander was referring to a high-ranking security officer from the corps?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the members of the security organ at the brigade level, that is at the Zvornik Brigade, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us who you are aware of were members of the security organ at the brigade level at that time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic was the security officer. Everybody knew that. All those who were mobilised knew that he was the security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name Milorad Trbic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were in the same battalion. I forgot about him. He was also up there. He held a position of some kind. He was sitting alongside with him, but I don't know what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say "up there" what do you mean? In the transcript it reads --

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the brigade. When you say "up there" you mean the brigade, so not at our level but up there, at their level.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And was he a member of the security organ at the brigade level as well?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what he did. I know that he was in the brigade, but I don't know what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned just a little while ago, and I promised we would get back to this, a telephone call that you received the night that your commander told you about the prisoners at the school. What I wanted to ask you about was the telegram that you testified about that the command received that night. And that's at page 13374 of your testimony in the Popovic case. Can you just tell us briefly how that telegram arrived, or the circumstances under which it arrived at the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was during the night, at 12, perhaps 1, nobody actually checked the time. We had an induction telephone line with the brigade, and the telephone rang. All the telegrams that we received arrived from the Zvornik Brigade. By the telephone there was a notebook where we recorded the contents of all the telegrams we received or sent to the brigade. During that night, a telegram came, it was coded. We were at the command. Nobody who was there could decode it. Men from the communications came and they decoded the contents of the telegram. The request upon us was to assign people who would execute the prisoners, and after all that, the commander mustered the courage to disobey the order and sent back a telegram stating that he would never assign any of his men to carry out that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That night, do you have a recollection of who was present at the battalion command, which members of the command were around that night?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I said already that I can't remember everybody who was there, but we were mobilised a hundred per cent, that's why I think that everybody was there. I can't really give you all of their names, but it would be a fair description if I told you that we were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What I'd like to show you is 65 ter 299. Now, I know you've seen this before. It is the Attendance of Battalion Command Personnel, it's entitled, the Attendance of Battalion Command Personnel in Performance of Combat Tasks. It's for the month of July 1995, and it refers to the 2nd Infantry Battalion. What I'd like you to do is I'd like you to take a look at the names. Maybe we can blow up -- we should blow up the B/C/S version of it and we can just focus in on the names. That would be the best way to do it. Just blow up the name side of it so that he can read it. Thank you very much. All right. What we should have here are the members of the command listed; is that right, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And we have what appears to be 16 entries that read Srecko Acimovic, Commander; Stevo Savic. Do you know what his position was back in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He was demobilised, so the answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, what was his position when he was mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Deputy commander, and Srecko Acimovic was commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we have Sakotic, Milorad, and it says OBP. Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He was our security officer in the battalion, and at that moment he was on duty in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we have Vujo Lazarevic, and it says "morale." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He was the assistant commander for moral guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then we have, looks like Lisic, Zivan?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Pisic, Zivan Pisic, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And his position was?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He was the assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then we have you at number 6; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to go through all of the names here, but these would have been -- these individuals named here would have made up the command in July 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Beneath that, we see Communications. It should say Veza there. Do you see that, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And under Communications, we have Stevanovic, Dragan. Can you tell us what his position was back in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They were all communications guys. I don't know what each of them did, I only know that they were assigned to the communications department.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And those individuals we have here numbered 1 through 8 as Pisic, Miodrag; Ilic, Goran; Cvijetinovic, Milisav; Galic, Pero; Peric, Milos; Ljubic, Srecko; and Milic Sveto; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: These would have been the signallers back in July 1995, yes?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you mentioned that a signalsman had to be called to the brigade battalion command in order to decode the telegram that had been received from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that it would have been one of those eight individuals, at least, to have come to the command for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you have any specific recollection about seeing any one of those individuals in the command the day that that telegram arrived, or that night?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Somebody decoded the telegram, but I don't know who that was. I know that somebody had come from the communications department, a signalsman came, and I really can't remember who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With the exhibit number P1442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that the commander, Acimovic, had a telegram sent back to the brigade command. Was that telegram, to your knowledge, recorded in the logbook at the battalion level?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think it was. All the telegrams that were either received or sent were recorded in that notebook. It was just a common notebook that normally was there by the telephone itself and one generally recorded everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would that have been recorded by a member of the command, that is someone such as yourself, or would it have been recorded by a communications officer?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Someone from the command would dictate a text for the brigade. Someone from the command. It might have been me. I just can't remember, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And who would have entered this telegram in the logbook? Who would have written that information down?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Someone from the command. One of us who were there. But I can't say who specifically. At the time, there was no one keeping any sorts of records at all. The situation was chaotic. It wasn't really a priority for anyone at the time, this sort of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: After the commander sent this reply telegram to the brigade command, in your testimony you say that he received a phone call. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know from whom he received this telephone call?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Someone from the brigade who was pressuring him to make some people available, some men available. They got into an altercation and he told the other guy that he would never make any men available to him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was there any subsequent phone call?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. This was late at night. It might have been 2.00 or 3.00, or 4 perhaps, I don't remember. Someone called him but I don't know who exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know how long this phone call went on, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that degree of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did your commander at any point, and I don't mean necessarily that particular evening, but did he at any point ever tell you whom he had this conversation with the night that the telegram arrived at the battalion command? Did he ever mention that to you in casual conversation or any time after that period?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I do not wish to commit regarding something that I'm not sure about. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, that morning, I believe you testified that the commander went to the school. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he go to the school by himself or did he go with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And about what time did he go, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sometime that morning. I don't know specifically what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I don't think you were asked this before, but can you tell us about how long he was away from the battalion command after he left?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not long, I think. The point of him going there was to go and say that he would not be sending any men over for that purpose. That was why he went there. Again, there was an altercation; he was being pressured into doing something, so he went there himself to make it clear to them that he would not be making any men available. How long did he stay there for? Not long, I think, but I don't know how long exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to approximate? An hour, two hours, five hours, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps about two hours, three hours. Certainly not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your prior testimony you mentioned that when he came back he spoke about having met a member of the corps or, rather, a high-ranking member of the Drina Corps security organ. Did he tell you who that person was that he met at that time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember that kind of detail. He told me that he would be summoned by the military court to answer for not making any men available. He said, "I'll be court-martialed for this."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he tell you if there were any other members of the corps or other members VRS units at the school when he went there that morning?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. Nor did I ask him, truth to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall when it was that you first heard that the prisoners at the school had been transported to be executed?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was after all those events. Whoever lived in the area had heard about those people being shot. Was it two, three, four, or seven days after, again, this is not something that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you hear about this from your commander or other members of your battalion or did you hear about this just casually in the neighbourhood, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I heard on a more casual basis. I think everybody knew about that several days later, about the fact that that had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to go into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you heard about the prisoners that had been executed in Kozluk, the ones that were detained in Rocevic, was that something that was common knowledge within the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, a day or two later people heard about it, what had been done, and there was no one in the entire area who didn't know. We are not just talking about the command here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Mr. Lazarevic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would just put a question to you, sir. I take it that Mr. Acimovic was your commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just at the end of the examination by Mr. Vanderpuye, you were -- you answered on page 82, line 10 to 12: "He told me that he would be summoned by the military court to answer for not making any men available. He said, 'I'll be court --" and that is recorded incorrectly -- "-martialed for this." Can you tell me what happened to Mr. Acimovic after this event? Do you know anything about him and his whereabouts and what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one ever called him to account for that. It had been an insane order. Why would anyone have held him responsible for that? It was a madman's idea to have those people killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just need two clarifications. The first one is in answer to this question: "And just so we are clear for the record, is it the case that the dead people that he was talking about were, in fact, the prisoners?" And your answer is, "Yes." How do you know that? How do you know they were prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that from the commander, when he came the first evening, that they had taken out several people and shot them. I heard from the commander. That's why he called the responsible people at the brigade, to prevent that, to stop that from happening, and to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was in private session. If we turn back into private session, and that part will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn for the day, but I see Mr. Vanderpuye on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President. I just wanted to, for the Court's information -- you know what? Never mind. It's something that I can't reveal at this time anyway but -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If there is a need for that, we can deal with that perhaps tomorrow. We have -- we are already over time, some minutes after 7.00. We have to adjourn for the day. Sir, the Court Usher will assist you. We resume tomorrow morning in this courtroom. Please be advised that you are not allowed to have contact about the content of your testimony with either party. Thank you very much. We adjourn and resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
